title: Rook pawn: the draw
summary: The rook pawn's two key squares, the race of the kings and the defences that save half a point.
part.keySquares.title: The key squares
part.keySquares.summary: g7 and g8 for the attacker; f7 and f8 for the defender, and the white king gets locked in the corner.
part.race.title: Panno versus Najdorf
part.race.summary: One king runs for g7, the other for f8: count the moves and check whose turn it is.
part.kingFirst.title: King first
part.kingFirst.summary: The pawn waits; the king steps into the black king's path and shoulders it away.
part.summary.title: Barcza versus Fischer
part.summary.summary: Barcza against Fischer, the square where the pawn falls, and the rules for your games.
step.t_keys: In the king and pawn lesson you saw that the king in the corner draws. Here the black king hasn't got there yet, and it is one step from f8. Which white king move wins, and why do almost all the others draw?
step.t_keys.hint1: Forget the pawn for a moment. What does the black king want to do on its next move?
step.t_keys.hint2: Look at the two squares next to the corner, g7 and g8. Whoever gets close to them first decides.
step.keys: A rook pawn has only two key squares, and they never change: g7 and g8. Pawn on h2 or on h6, it makes no difference. Once my king steps on one of them, the black king never reaches the corner again, and the pawn walks up, as long as the black king doesn't catch it first. That is why 1.Kg7! (1.Kg8 also wins.) The black king is left outside.
step.d_keys: See how simple it is when the white king arrives first. The black king chases the pawn and never catches it.
step.d_keys.m1: 1.Kg7. The king enters the key square and shuts the corner.
step.d_keys.m2: 1...Ke7. f8 is shut by my king on g7, and the black king moves away from the corner.
step.d_keys.m3: 2.h4. Now the pawn moves; the king on g7 looks after its path.
step.d_keys.m4: 2...Ke6. With f8 gone, the black king goes after the pawn.
step.d_keys.m5: 3.h5. The pawn keeps going; from e6, the black king is too late.
step.d_keys.m6: 3...Kf5. It threatens 4...Kg5 and capturing the pawn.
step.d_keys.m7: 4.h6! It is the only move: the pawn runs to the square my king protects, and promotes.
step.keysMove: Your turn. The black king wants to come back via e7 and e8. Shoulder it before you touch the pawn.
step.keysMove.hint: Put your king on a square that takes e7 and e8 from the black king, right next to the road to g7.
step.keysMove.done: That's it. With 1.Kf7 (or 1.Kf6) Black never reaches f8, and the pawn walks up in peace.
step.d_lock: I'll defend with Black. Notice that, once on f7, my king only steps between f7 and f8.
step.d_lock.m1: 1...Kf7. I shut g7 and g8 at once.
step.d_lock.m2: 2.h6. White pushes the pawn, because the king can only shuffle between h8 and h7.
step.d_lock.m3: 2...Kf8, no hurry: g7 and g8 stay shut.
step.d_lock.m4: 3.h7. Now the white king has no square at all.
step.d_lock.m5: 3...Kf7, and White has no move: stalemate. Draw.
step.lockMove: The white king is in the corner. Get there in time to lock it in.
step.lockMove.hint: Head for the f-file, close to g7 and g8, and stay around there.
step.lockMove.done: Perfect. The white king is locked in the corner, and the pawn alone can do nothing.
step.t_panno: Panno against Najdorf, Buenos Aires, 1968, in a seniors-against-juniors event. Najdorf took the a6 pawn with 56...Rxa6, Panno traded rooks with 57.Rxa6 Kxa6, captured Black's last pawn with 58.Kxh3, and Najdorf played 58...Kb7. Both kings are far from the corner. Who wins the race?
step.t_panno.hint1: Count how many moves the white king needs to reach g7, and how many the black king needs to reach f8.
step.t_panno.hint2: Both need four moves. So whose turn it is decides.
step.panno: This is a race, and the pawn takes no part in it. The white king heads for g7, the black king for f8. White climbs the g-file, Black walks along the seventh rank, and both are four moves away. With White to move, the white king gets there first. Najdorf, one of the greats of his time, had just played 58...Kb7 and was already lost.
step.d_panno: The game, and what would have followed. Panno wastes no time on the pawn.
step.d_panno.m1: 59.Kg4. The race begins; the pawn waits on h2.
step.d_panno.m2: 59...Kc7. Najdorf runs too, along the seventh rank; three moves to go to f8.
step.d_panno.m3: 60.Kg5, and here Najdorf resigned. The rest is analysis.
step.d_panno.m4: 60...Kd7. Had he played on, the black king would be two moves from f8.
step.d_panno.m5: 61.Kg6. The white king already covers f7 and is one move from g7.
step.d_panno.m6: 61...Ke7. One step from f8, but it is White's move.
step.d_panno.m7: 62.Kg7! It is the only winning move: the black king is left outside, and 63.h4 brings the pawn home.
step.pannoDraw: What if it were Black to move? The count is the same, four moves each, but now the black king starts first.
step.pannoDraw.hint: Walk along the seventh rank to e7, then step to f8.
step.pannoDraw.done: You made it. King on f8, and the white king never steps on g7. That is what Najdorf lacked: the move.
step.t_shoulder: Now you are the attacker, and the black king is far away. The black king is on e4, far from the corner, and the pawn is still on h3. Pushing the pawn looks natural. Which move wins?
step.t_shoulder.hint1: Where does the black king want to go? It has to pass through the f-file.
step.t_shoulder.hint2: Think of a king move that stands in the black king's way, not one that runs straight to g7.
step.shoulder: The reflex of pushing the pawn spoils everything: 1.h4? Kf5 2.h5 Kf6, and the black king reaches f7. The right move is 1.Kg6! It is the only one: my king does not run to g7, it steps into the way and takes f5, f6 and f7. This is called the shoulder: with its body, one king pushes the other away.
step.d_shoulder: See how the black king has to take the long way round.
step.d_shoulder.m1: 1.Kg6! The squares f5, f6 and f7 are mine now.
step.d_shoulder.m2: 1...Ke5. The black king tries the middle road, via e6 and e7.
step.d_shoulder.m3: 2.h4. Now the pawn moves; from e5, the black king can no longer catch it.
step.d_shoulder.m4: 2...Ke6. It looks for e7 and f8, the defending square.
step.d_shoulder.m5: 3.h5. The pawn keeps going; after 3...Ke7 comes 4.Kg7, and the black king is left outside.
step.exception: 1.h7! The pawn takes g8, my king takes g7, and the black king cannot reach the square in front of the pawn: White wins. If it were Black to move, the king would go to g8 and, after the pawn advances with check, to h8, and the white king could only protect the pawn by giving stalemate. That is the defence in the corner: stalemate. It only works if Black has no other move.
step.barcza: Now the other side of the board and the other side of the table. Barcza against Fischer, Zurich, 1959. Barcza's pawn had stood on a4 since 55.a4, blocking Fischer's on a5. Both sides queened, and after a long series of checks Fischer took the a4 pawn with 94...Qxa4, the queens came off with 95.Qxa4+ Kxa4, and he was left with the a5 pawn against Barcza's lone king. The square the white king needs is c1, f8's twin for a pawn going down. The white king arrives in time with 96.Kd2 and 97.Kc1, which is why the game ended in a draw here.
step.barczaMove: Take the king to c1, as Barcza would, then to b1.
step.barczaMove.hint: Go down the diagonal towards c1. Don't let the black king reach b2 before you.
step.barczaMove.done: Done. The white king is on b1, next to the corner, and Fischer has no way to drive it out.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: the rook pawn has two key squares, g7 and g8; the defender draws on f8, f7 or in front of the pawn, and from there locks the white king in the corner. Second: it is a race of kings; count the moves, check whose turn it is, and don't walk alongside the enemy king, or it shoulders you away. Third: count the pawns too: the one that will fall still gains time, the one left after a trade decides, stalemate only saves the side that has no other move, and with two rook pawns, block your opponent's pawn far from the corner.
step.finish: The h5 pawn is going to fall, but the black king wants to use that time to reach f8. Shut its road before you capture.
ex.e10: The black king is on the other side of the board. Is there still time? Find the draw.
ex.e10.hint: The shortest road to f8 is a diagonal. Count the moves.
ex.e10.solution: 1...Kc3!, 2...Kd4 and 3...Ke5: the black king crosses the board along the diagonal and reaches f7 or f8 in time. Any other first move loses a tempo, and that tempo decides.
ex.e12: Your pawn is going to fall, and the white king is closer to the corner. What is the pawn worth before it falls? Find the draw.
ex.e12.hint: The black king must reach f8. The white king spends moves to capture a pawn; make it spend as many as possible.
ex.e12.solution: 1...Kc5!, and the king goes on along the diagonal: 3...Kd6, 4...Ke7, 5...Kf8. After 2.Kg7, only 2...h5! holds: the white king needs two moves to fetch the pawn (3.Kg6 and 4.Kxh5), and the black king reaches f8. With the pawn left on h7 (2...Kd6?), 3.Kxh7 and 4.Kg7 come first. The other first moves arrive one tempo late.
ex.e13: A pawn trade is coming. Which of your pawns do you want to keep? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: Remember what a rook pawn is worth with the black king near the corner. The other pawn has real key squares.
ex.e13.solution: 1.h5! (1.Kf6 also wins). After 1...gxh5 2.Kxh5 the f-pawn is left, and the white king goes in front of it (3.Kg5, 4.Kf5): an ordinary king and pawn ending, won. 1.f5? gxf5 leaves White with the h-pawn and the black king one step from h8: a draw. 1.Kg4 also lets the win slip.
ex.e15: Study by Moravec, Československý šach, 1952. White to move and win. The pawns are going to meet. Think about the pawn that will be left.
ex.e15.hint: If your g-pawn captures on h3, it becomes a rook pawn and the black king still reaches f8. King first, and the pawn only at the right moment.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kf2! h4 2.Kg1! h3 and only now 3.g3! The black pawn is stuck on h3 and falls (4.Kh2 and 5.Kxh3), and the pawn that is left is the g-pawn, which wins. The other roads fail: 1.g3? and Black holds, for example with 1...h4; 1.Kg1? Kd7 and Black brings the king instead of advancing; 1.Kf2 h4 2.Kf3? h3! and 3.gxh3 gives a rook pawn again. If Black brings the king at once (1.Kf2 Kd7), only 2.Kg3 wins.
ex.e14: The a7 pawn is lost. The black king must reach c7 in time to lock the white king in the corner. Which way? Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: The white king will fetch the pawn via d6, c7 and b7. If the black king runs alongside it, it gets shouldered away. Sometimes arriving later means arriving in time.
ex.e14.solution: 1...Kf3!!, the only move. The black king waits far away, on a square where the white king cannot block it, and then comes in behind it: 2.Kd6 Kf4 3.Kc7 Ke5 4.Kb7 Kd6 5.Kxa7 Kc7, and the white king is locked on a7 and a8. The natural 1...Kd3? loses: 2.Kd5! takes c4, d4 and e4, the black king has to go around (2...Kc3 3.Kc6 Kb4 4.Kb7) and arrives too late. 1...Kd2, 1...Ke2 and 1...Kf2 also lose.
ex.e16: Study by Grigoriev, 1920. White to move and draw. The h3 pawn is going to fall and the black king is closer to it. Is there still a way out?
ex.e16.hint: In the end each side will have a rook pawn. Decide now which a-pawn survives and on which square.
ex.e16.solution: 1.a4!! first: the a5 pawn is fixed. Then the white king goes down the f-file to f1 (2.Ke6, 3.Kf5, 4.Kf4, 5.Kf3, 6.Kf2, 7.Kf1, all of them the only move) and locks the black king on h2 and h1, as in the chapter about the king locked in the corner, with the colours reversed. When the black king steps out, White takes the h3 pawn, and when Black goes for the a4 pawn (13...Kxa4), the white king is on e3: it is the Barcza–Fischer position, and 14.Kd2 and 15.Kc1 draw. After 1.Ke6?, Black plays 1...a4! and wins the a3 pawn with the king near Black's own corner.
ex.e17: Study by Grigoriev, 1954. White to move and win. With the black king in the corner, the h-pawn alone only draws. But Black has pawns. How do you use that?
ex.e17.hint: Bring the king near the corner first. Then count: when the pawn reaches h7, whose move should it be?
ex.e17.solution: 1.Ke6, 2.Kf6 and 3.Kg6 (all forced), and then 4.h3! (or 4.Kf6, which also waits). The pawn walks square by square, 5.h4, 6.h5, 7.h6 and 8.h7, and arrives without check, with the black king on h8 and Black to move. The black king has no move; without pawns it would be stalemate, but Black must move a pawn (8...d5), the white king goes after them (9.Kf5, 10.Ke5, 11.Kxd5) and wins. With 4.h4? at once, the pawn reaches h7 with check and White to move, and then it is a draw.
key.keys: With a rook pawn only two squares matter: the two next to the corner, on the neighbouring file. If the white king gets there, it wins; if the black king gets near the corner first, it draws. Here, the side to move decides.
key.lock: The white king is stuck in the corner, in front of its own pawn. The black king only has to hover alongside and it never gets out: a draw.
key.pannoNajdorf: Panno against Najdorf, Buenos Aires 1968: both kings race for the corner. With White to move, the white king gets there first and wins; with Black to move, the black king would arrive in time. Panno had the move.
key.shoulder: King first, pawn later: the white king steps across and blocks the black king's path. If the pawn moves first, the black king reaches the corner and draws.
key.exception: The exception: with the pawn already far advanced and White to move, it steps forward once more, the white king guards the square in front, and the black king never reaches the corner. White wins.
key.barczaFischer: Barcza against Fischer, Zurich 1959: Fischer had the extra pawn, but Barcza's king was close enough to the corner. The game ended in a draw here.
history: The rook pawn, the one on the edge of the board, is the worst pawn to have and the best one to face. With a central pawn, king and pawn against king often wins; with a rook pawn, the defending king only has to reach the corner and the game is drawn. It saves half points remarkably often, and many experienced players have thrown away a win without noticing that the corner was a safe harbour for the opponent. In Zurich, 1959, Barcza saved the draw against the young Fischer because his king could still reach the corner in time. In Buenos Aires, 1968, Najdorf reached the same kind of ending, but one move too late: Panno got his king there first and Najdorf resigned.
practice: Now the practical challenge. You defend with Black, and the white king is closer to the pawn. Count the moves, find the shortest road to f8 and hold the draw.
part.behind.title: Coming from behind
part.behind.summary: The defender doesn't run alongside the attacking king: it comes from behind.
part.decoy.title: The pawn that falls
part.decoy.summary: The pawn that will fall is still worth moves: make the white king spend them.
part.whichPawn.title: Which pawn is left
part.whichPawn.summary: In a trade, look at the pawn that is left: the rook pawn draws.
part.theTurn.title: The move in the corner
part.theTurn.summary: Stalemate saves the king in the corner, but only if it has no other move.
step.lock: The same position with Black to move. 1...Kf7! My king loses g7 and g8, the only squares by which it could step out of the pawn's way. If it stays, it is locked in; if it retreats, the black king walks into the corner. For the defender the rule is the mirror image: reaching f8, f7 or the square in front of the pawn already draws.
step.t_behind: Now you defend with Black. The white king will fetch your a6 pawn via d5, c6 and b6. After the capture it stands on a6, and your king must be on c6 or c7 to lock it in there. The shortest road seems to be via c2 or d2. Where does your king go?
step.t_behind.hint1: What does the white king do if your king goes to the d-file?
step.t_behind.hint2: It steps in front, as in the shoulder chapter, and your king has to go round.
step.t_behind.hint3: Look for a square from which the white king cannot block you, even if it seems to go backwards.
step.behind: The white king needs four moves to capture on a6: d5, c6, b6 and a6. The black king needs five to reach c6, but that is enough, because it arrives on the move after the capture and the white king is locked in. The danger is the road: alongside the white king, it gets shouldered. That is why 1...Ke2! It looks like the wrong direction, but from there the black king comes in behind, via e3, d4 and d5, to c6, and nobody can block it.
step.behindErr: First the natural mistake: 1...Kd2? It runs towards the c-file, but 2.Kd4! takes c3, d3 and e3. That is the shoulder: the black king has to go round via c2 and b3, and reaches c7 one move too late.
step.d_behind: Now the right way, move by move.
step.d_behind.m1: 1...Ke2! The black king steps away from d2, where it would be shouldered.
step.d_behind.m2: 2.Kd5. The white king goes for the pawn.
step.d_behind.m3: 2...Ke3. The black king follows from behind, never alongside the white one.
step.d_behind.m4: 3.Kc6. Two moves left to capture; the black king follows at a distance, never alongside the white one, so it does not get shouldered.
step.d_behind.m5: 3...Kd4. Always one diagonal behind the white king.
step.d_behind.m7: 4...Kd5! The only move that holds: after 5.Kxa6 comes 5...Kc6, and the white king is locked on a6 and a7.
step.behindMove: The white king will fetch the a5 pawn via c4 and b5. Arrive later, but in time.
step.behindMove.hint: Don't stay near the white king, or it blocks your road. Step away and come in from behind.
step.behindMove.done: That's it. 1...Kf2!, 2...Ke3, 3...Kd4 and 4...Kc5: the white king captures on a5 and is locked in.
step.t_decoy: So far only White had a pawn. The white king is on g7, right next to your pawn, and your king is on c6, far from the corner. The h7 pawn is going to fall. How do you gain time to reach f8?
step.t_decoy.hint1: Count how many moves the white king spends to capture the pawn and get back to g7.
step.t_decoy.hint2: With the pawn on h7, it is a single move, and the white king stays on g7.
step.t_decoy.hint3: The farther away the pawn is, the more moves the white king spends, and the farther from g7 it gets.
step.decoy: This pawn will fall, but it is still worth time. On h7, the white king captures it in one move and is already on g7. The move is 1...h5! Now the white king needs two moves, 2.Kg6 and 3.Kxh5, and it leaves g7 behind. In those two moves, the black king goes to d6 and e7, and reaches f8 in time.
step.decoyErr: The mistake is to run straight away: 1...Kd6? Now 2.Kxh7 costs a single move, and after 2...Ke7 3.Kg7 the white king is already on the key square. The h3 pawn walks up on its own.
step.d_decoy.m1: 1...h5! The pawn moves away from the white king.
step.d_decoy.m2: 2.Kg6. The white king goes after it, and g7 is left behind.
step.d_decoy.m3: 2...Kd6. The black king runs for the corner.
step.d_decoy.m5: 3...Ke7. Now the black king is close: after 4.Kg6 comes 4...Kf8, and it is a draw.
step.decoyMove: The h6 pawn is going to fall. Make the white king spend as many moves as possible.
step.decoyMove.hint: If the white king takes on h6 in one move, it gets back to g7 in time. Move the pawn away.
step.decoyMove.done: That's it. 1...h5! cost the white king two moves, and your king reached f8.
step.t_which: Now White's pawn is not a rook pawn. The white king is going to capture your h4 pawn, and the g2 pawn looks like it wins by itself. There is a move that changes which white pawn is left. Which one?
step.t_which.hint1: You won't save your pawn. Think about the white pawn that will be left.
step.t_which.hint2: White's g-pawn has real key squares; the h-pawn doesn't.
step.t_which.hint3: Before it falls, your pawn can still force the g-pawn to do something.
step.which: In a pawn trade, look at what is left. 1...h3! forces 2.gxh3, otherwise the black pawn captures on g2 or runs on to h2 and promotes. The white pawn that is left is a rook pawn, and the black king runs for f8. After 1...Ke5? comes 2.Kxh4, and the g-pawn, with the white king beside it, wins.
step.d_which.m1: 1...h3! The pawn offers itself, so that the g-pawn has to capture and become a rook pawn.
step.d_which.m2: 2.gxh3. It is the only move: without it, White loses. Now the white pawn is a rook pawn.
step.d_which.m3: 2...Ke7. The black king runs for the corner.
step.d_which.m4: 3.Kg6. The white king cannot get to g7 first.
step.d_which.m5: 3...Kf8. It is the defending square, and it is a draw.
step.whichMove: Now the other side: you attack. A capture is right there. Is it good?
step.whichMove.hint: If you capture on h5, which pawn is left?
step.whichMove.done: That's it. 1.g5! keeps the g-pawn, protected by the h4 pawn. After 1.gxh5+? Kxh5 only the rook pawn would be left, with the black king in front of it: a draw.
step.t_exception: White king on g6, pawn on h6, black king on f8. So far, f8 drew. But it is What changes?
step.t_exception.hint1: The black king needs g7 or g8. Who controls those squares now?
step.t_exception.hint2: Think about what would happen if it were Black to move.
step.d_spare: The black king is in the corner, the pawn is on h7 and my king on g6, with Black to move. Without other pawns, it would be stalemate. But Black has the c7 pawn.
step.d_spare.m1: 1...c5. The black king has no square, so the pawn has to move.
step.d_spare.m2: 2.b6. My pawn goes past, and the black king is still trapped.
step.d_spare.m3: 2...c4. Once more, the pawn has to move.
step.d_spare.m4: 3.b7. Black can only play 3...c3, and 4.b8=Q is mate. The h7 pawn traps the king; the c7 pawn took the stalemate away.
step.spareMove: The black pawn has just arrived on c6. Capturing looks natural.
step.spareMove.hint: If you capture on c6, which move is left for Black?
step.spareMove.done: That's it. 1.bxc6? would give stalemate, because Black would have no move at all. 1.b6! keeps the black pawn alive, and it has to move.
key.behind: The defender doesn't run alongside the attacking king, or it gets shouldered away. It waits a little way off and comes in from behind, in time to lock the other king in the corner.
key.decoy: The defender's pawn is going to fall, but it is still worth time: by moving away, it makes the attacking king spend moves to fetch it, and the other king reaches the corner.
key.whichPawn: When pawns are traded, what matters is the one that is left. The defender offers its pawn so that the opponent is left with an edge pawn, which only draws.
step.barczaErr: The straight road does not work. After 96.Kd3? comes 96...Kb3!, and after 97.Kd2 Kb2! the black king shuts c1 and c2 before the white one. The pawn walks down on its own. Against a pawn going down, the white king needs the diagonal to c1, without losing a single move.
step.contrastMove: Now switch sides. It is Barcza's position, but with Black's pawn and king one square further, on a4 and a3. The white king has already gone to d2, Barcza's road.
step.contrastMove.hint: Get to White's defending squares, c1 and c2, first.
step.contrastMove.done: That's it. 1...Kb2! shut c1 and c2, and the pawn walked down on its own. One square more decided it: that is why Barcza blocked Fischer's pawn on a5 with 55.a4. With two rook pawns, block your opponent's pawn far from the corner.
